title: Who is greater than you?
told: the history and tradition of Guru Tegh Bahadur, 1675

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever stood up for someone who wasn’t like you?
options: then this story is yours too. listen.
then let’s find out together. listen.

steps.line: 1675. A group of Hindu pandits from Kashmir arrived at Anandpur, worn out. Back home, they were being forced to give up their faith.
steps.label: from Sikh history and tradition

steps.line: They begged the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, for help. He listened, and grew quiet. Tradition says he told them it would take the sacrifice of a great soul.

steps.q: His nine-year-old son walks in and sees the pandits’ worried faces. What do you think the boy does first?
o: Asks his father what is wrong
Runs to bring his mother in
Sits down quietly with the pandits
steps.why: He asks what’s wrong. The boy was Gobind Rai, born far to the east in Patna; he had come to Anandpur only a few years before.

steps.line: His son Gobind, nine years old, asked what was wrong. Then he said: who is greater than you, father, to do this?
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: So the Guru went to Delhi to speak for their freedom. He would not give up his faith, or let theirs be taken. There he was put to death.

steps.q: He wasn’t a Hindu. Why give his life for Hindus’ freedom to worship?
o: He hoped they would become Sikhs
Their freedom mattered, not just his own
The emperor had ordered him to come
steps.why: Sikhs remember him as Hind di Chadar, the shield of India, for dying for other people’s freedom of faith.

steps.line: Sikhs honor him as a martyr for other people’s freedom. A gurdwara, Sis Ganj, stands in Delhi where he died.
steps.label: today

steps.line: That boy became Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru. He taught that a Sikh should be sant sipahi: saint and soldier.

steps.q: In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh called a great gathering. What did he ask the crowd for first?
o: Every family’s best horse and sword
Gold to build a new fortress
A volunteer willing to give his head
steps.why: Five stepped forward, one by one, from different castes and regions. They became the Panj Pyare, the Five Beloved, the first of the Khalsa.

steps.q: After the execution, Bhai Jaita carried the Guru’s head back to Anandpur in secret. How did young Gobind greet him?
o: He gave him land and a fine horse
He embraced him as the Guru’s own son
He asked him to keep it a secret
steps.why: Tradition remembers his words: “Rangrete Guru ke bete,” the Rangretas are the Guru’s own sons. Jaita came from a caste others looked down on.

say: sant sipahi, saint and soldier, and the order matters. saint first: remembrance, humility, the name.
and soldier, because when the weak are being crushed, a saint doesn’t look away. a soldier with no saint in him is only violence. the kirpan comes from exactly this.

steps.q: From the story, what is the soldier half of sant sipahi there to protect?
o: Other people’s freedom, of any faith
Only the Sikh community and its land
The Guru’s own throne and power
steps.why: His father showed him: stand for others, even when they aren’t your own.

today.say: today, notice one person near you who believes differently, and quietly be on their side: include them, speak up for them, or ask about their faith with real interest.
options: good. noticing is where the soldier’s half begins.

card.keepWhy: Who is greater than you, to stand for someone else?
sources: Sikh tradition of the Kashmiri pandits, led by Pandit Kirpa Ram, petitioning Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur (then called Chak Nanaki; the common name is used), 1675, and young Gobind Rai’s words
Martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur in Delhi, 1675; Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib, Chandni Chowk
check: The boy’s words (“who is greater than you”) and the Guru’s words about a great soul are tradition; wording varies.
The execution is kept off-screen (“put to death”), gently.
